description:
Hi! I’m Sumbal Zehra, a Computer Systems Engineering student building a solo entry for the NASA Space Apps MODIS & VIIRS Hotspot Harmonization challenge.

I’m developing an end-to-end framework to align spatial resolutions, filter false positives, and normalize fire confidence scores.
summary: FireRhythm is a web application that turns two generations of NASA satellite fire data into one consistent burning-activity calendar. MODIS (since 2000, 1 km) and VIIRS (since 2012, 375 m) detect fire differently: VIIRS sees 3–8 times more hotspots, so splicing the records creates a false jump in 2012. I treat each sensor as a measuring system and use machine learning (LightGBM) to learn the MODIS-to-VIIRS transfer function on their overlap years, then rebuild 2000–2012 as VIIRS-equivalents. This cut error by 23% versus a fixed conversion ratio and removed the 2012 jump (p = 3×10⁻¹¹ → 0.07). Signal processing (STL, FFT) then fingerprints each area’s fire rhythm and discovers burning regimes without a land-cover map. Applied to the Punjab rice–wheat belt, FireRhythm shows when burning peaks, flags unusual activity, forecasts the season and ranks where to send crop-residue machinery first. Users can draw any area, view the calendar, compare the current month with history, see live NASA FIRMS detections and download CSVs. This helps agriculture, environment and disaster agencies act before smoke and fire spread.
details:
FireRhythm is a web application that turns two generations of NASA satellite fire data into one consistent burning-activity calendar, then uses it for early warning. MODIS (2000 to now, 1 km pixels) and VIIRS (2012 to now, 375 m pixels) detect fires differently: VIIRS sees 3 to 8 times more hotspots. Joining the records naively creates a false jump in fire activity in 2012, so past and present burning can’t be compared. FireRhythm removes that artifact and builds a consistent record from 2000 to today for the Punjab rice–wheat belt (Pakistan and India), on a grid of 648 cells at 0.25 degrees.

How it works

  1. Ingestion. We downloaded about 25 years of MODIS and VIIRS hotspots from the NASA FIRMS API, filtered them to vegetation fires and reliable detections, and counted them per grid cell per month.
  2. Harmonization as system identification. We treat each sensor as a measuring system that filters the true fire signal; MODIS acts like a coarse, low-pass view. On the years when both sensors observed together, a LightGBM model learns the MODIS-to-VIIRS transfer function from fire intensity (FRP), day/night mix, season and location. We then apply it to the MODIS-only years. On held-out years (2023 onward), it cut cell-level error by 23% compared with a fixed conversion ratio and raised regional R² from 0.68 to 0.83.
  3. Validation. Change-point detection and a t-test show the 2012 jump disappears: p = 3×10⁻¹¹ for the naive record, p = 0.069 after harmonization.
  4. Signal fingerprints. STL decomposition and the FFT describe each cell’s fire rhythm: 6- and 12-month amplitude, phase and spectral entropy. K-means clustering then discovers burning regimes without any land-cover map. It correctly isolates the rice–wheat belt, which peaks in October–November and May, with a typical burning onset of 19 October.
    • a robust anomaly score versus the same month in past years
    • how early the burning season has started
    • a LightGBM forecast of next month, with SHAP explanations

What the app offers

Users can draw any area on a map or enter coordinates. They can then:

  • view the year-by-month burn calendar
  • compare the current month with the historical median
  • explore fire regimes and the risk map
  • download hotspots and priority lists as CSV

A live map shows exact detection points, a heatmap, or 3D hexbins and 3D risk columns. It runs on archived data or on live NASA FIRMS detections from the last 1 to 5 days, using VIIRS S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and MODIS.

Benefits and intended impact

FireRhythm gives fire, agriculture and environment agencies a consistent long-term picture of when and where burning happens. It shows which months and years were worst, and whether this month is unusual. In Punjab, crop-residue burning drives severe autumn smog. FireRhythm shows that October burning fell from 13,410 hotspots in 2023 to 7,577 in 2026, and that what remains is concentrated in the western belt. That helps target machinery, enforcement and public-health warnings where they matter most. The method transfers to any region and will keep working as MODIS is retired.

Tools and technologies

  • Language: Python
  • Data and analysis: pandas, NumPy, PyArrow/Parquet
  • Machine learning: LightGBM, scikit-learn (k-means), SHAP-style contributions
  • Signal processing and statistics: statsmodels (STL), SciPy (FFT), ruptures (PELT change-point detection)
  • App: Streamlit, with pydeck (deck.gl) for the live map, folium for drawing areas, and Plotly for charts
  • Deployment: Streamlit Community Cloud
  • Data: NASA FIRMS REST API
  • Version control: Git and GitHub
  • Diagrams and slides: Mermaid, PowerPoint/Canva

No special hardware was needed; everything ran on a laptop.

What makes it creative

  • Instead of a fixed scaling factor, we frame harmonization as a systems and signal-processing problem: learning a sensor’s transfer function. We then prove the result statistically, rather than just showing that the curves look similar.
  • We classify burn types from the rhythm of the signal itself, with no land-cover data.
  • We connect fire data to smart agriculture: a forecast of the burning window and a priority list for residue-management machinery.
  • We engineered it as a system. The repository includes requirements, architecture, an interface control table, trade studies, a traceability matrix with real test results, and a risk register.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about uncertainty. Pre-2012 values are labeled as modeled. MODIS had only the Terra satellite until 2002. Early-season recall of the risk flag is limited, and we report it.
  • Sensor aging. Orbit drift weakens MODIS detections in recent years.
  • Data quality. Static or industrial heat sources appear in near-real-time data, so the deployment list requires an established burning history.
  • Accessibility. All color scales are colorblind-safe.
  • Performance. The app reads precomputed files and only calls the API in live mode.
  • Future work. Weather inputs (ERA5), more regions, and SMS alerts for district officers.
